questions.question: Does CellAddress actually fit the store's read/write surface as H1 asserts?
questions.resolution: NO. H1's stated acceptance is unachievable as literally written. CellAddress carries six fields including class_id; every store entry point addresses a SLOT of k cells and is class-agnostic, taking the same five (driver, era, vocabulary, channel, what_measure). The class dimension comes from vocabulary.class_ids, and the k-cells-always-populated invariant depends on the method spanning all of them. The real data clump is the five-field slot; CellAddress is slot + class_id.
questions.code_evidence: src/physics/fingerprint/address.py:81-86 (six fields incl. class_id) vs src/physics/fingerprint/store.py:193-203 (write_fingerprint), :255-257 (get_fingerprint), :298-300 (row_count) — all five-field, class-agnostic.

questions.question: H1's acceptance ('store API typed on CellAddress') is unachievable as written. Is the binding intent the letter (force CellAddress with a dummy class_id) or the effect (any value-object address surface that makes an ill-formed address structurally unreachable)?
questions.resolution: The EFFECT. Introduce a five-field frozen SlotAddress (driver, era, vocabulary_version, channel, what_measure) validated by the rules CellAddress already enforces; re-express CellAddress as slot + class_id so there is one address ontology and one copy of the validation; type all three store methods on SlotAddress. Forcing the literal CellAddress would put a meaningless class_id on the signature and misdescribe what the method addresses.

questions.question: Is there a real validation hole, or is H1 purely cosmetic?
questions.resolution: Real and asymmetric. Write validates (it constructs a CellAddress per class before writing, so a malformed component raises). Read does not — get_fingerprint and row_count construct no address and bind primitives straight into the SELECT, so a malformed driver silently returns exactly k synthesized 'unresolved' cells, indistinguishable from a legitimate not-yet-fitted driver. That silent-wrong-answer shape is the first failure mode the project's own context file lists.
questions.code_evidence: src/physics/fingerprint/store.py:233-236 (write constructs CellAddress) and address.py:88-104 (the validation) vs store.py:255-296 + :298-312 (read paths construct nothing); store.py:277-285 is the silent miss-synthesis path; docs/agents/ORCHESTRATOR_CONTEXT.md:22 lists 'silent wrong prediction' first.

questions.question: May the retyped store API keep a primitives-accepting overload for a transition period, or is this a hard cutover?
questions.resolution: Hard cutover, no shim. The project rule is 'Prefer one clear execution path over compatibility shims or dual-format boundary acceptance', and an overload would preserve exactly the unvalidated path H1 exists to close. Cutover is mechanical: all call sites are positional, so a missed one is a TypeError at collect time, not a silent behaviour change. Two constructors keep call sites short — SlotAddress.for_vocabulary(driver, vocabulary, channel, what_measure), which derives era from vocabulary.rules_era, plus the explicit five-arg form that tests still need to exercise the era-mismatch refusal.

questions.question: Does the prescribed sys.path guard actually beat this repo's editable install, or is the prescribed fix ineffective?
questions.resolution: It works — verified from the installed hook's source rather than assumed. The editable install is the finder-hook flavour and maps 'src' to the MAIN checkout (confirming the trap), but its install() APPENDS the finder to sys.meta_path, so it sits after CPython's default PathFinder and sys.path is consulted first. sys.path.insert(0, repo_root) therefore wins. Had install() inserted at position 0, the prescribed fix would have been ineffective — that was the load-bearing unknown. The defect itself is confirmed: the script has no sys.path line and imports src.* three times.
questions.code_evidence: site-packages/__editable__.f1brainz-0.2.0.pth (one-line install() call); site-packages/__editable___f1brainz_0_2_0_finder.py MAPPING={'src': 'C:/Programs/f1Brainz/src'} and install() using sys.meta_path.append; scripts/fingerprint_class_coverage_675.py:98-100 (src.* imports) with no sys.path match anywhere in the file; house pattern at scripts/build_class_utilization_observables.py:71-75.

questions.question: Is H3's premise true — are the coverage/summary JSONs already ignored via '.agent-work/'?
questions.resolution: FALSE. .agent-work/ is a tracked directory; .gitignore covers only four named legacy subpaths plus *.pkl / *.npz / *.db / scratch/ / ckpt/ / backtests/ under it. Nothing covers *.json. Both named JSONs are in fact COMMITTED under the archive path, as are sibling artifacts from 664/667/669/670 — deliberately, per the repo's archive-then-commit convention. tc2's proposed blanket rule would silently un-track that evidence trail.
questions.code_evidence: .gitignore:241-254 and :283-288; git ls-files shows .agent-work/archive/2026-07-26-666-driver-fingerprint/artifacts/{bounded_fit_summary.json,coverage_675_verdict.json} tracked; docs/agents/engine-config.json rules_root 'Commit Commander work logs only after the work package is finished and archived under .agent-work/archive.'

questions.question: Given the premise is false, what is H3's correct disposition — blanket-ignore *.json under .agent-work (tc2 as written), narrow-ignore only the live pre-archive path, or fix the script's output anchoring?
questions.resolution: Reject the blanket rule; do both of the others. Blanket-ignoring would un-track committed evidence and contradict the archive-then-commit convention. The genuine stray risk is concrete: the 675 script writes to a bare RELATIVE path under the now-archived pre-archive work area and mkdir -p's it, so any rerun resurrects a stale, untracked, un-ignored directory inside a tracked tree at whatever cwd it ran from. Fix: anchor the script's output at the repo root (the same _REPO_ROOT the H2 guard introduces) and add an --out override, plus a narrow .gitignore rule for the live pre-archive artifact path.

questions.question: Does the read path's silent acceptance of a reserved what_measure get fixed here, given write refuses it?
questions.resolution: No — out of scope, route to triage. Adding a read-side refusal is a store behaviour change and the issue fences behaviour. The address object still tightens things usefully: an UNKNOWN what_measure will now be refused on read too, because CellAddress already validates membership; only the KNOWN-but-reserved case stays permissive, which is the deliberate dormant-slot design.
